name: Y Combinator
tagline: The accelerator that turned AI into a batch-scale asset class
summary: Founded in 2005 by Paul Graham, Jessica Livingston, Robert Morris and Trevor Blackwell and led today by president and CEO Garry Tan, Y Combinator is the template every other accelerator copies: two three-month batches a year in San Francisco, a standardised $500,000 deal, and a Demo Day that functions as the seed market's clearing house. Its AI position is unusual among investors — rather than concentrating capital in a handful of frontier labs, YC underwrites AI as a volume business, funding hundreds of application-layer and developer-tooling teams per year and letting the market select the winners. Since 2023 the large majority of each batch has described itself as AI-native, making YC the single widest funnel into early-stage AI.

thesis.heading: Volume over conviction
thesis.body: YC does not try to pick the one model company that wins. It writes the same cheque into hundreds of teams per year, accepts a high failure rate, and relies on batch scale plus follow-on rights to capture outliers — the opposite of the concentrated frontier bets made by growth funds.

thesis.heading: Application layer, not the model layer
thesis.body: Frontier training runs are far outside a $500K cheque. The portfolio clusters instead around products built on top of someone else's model: voice agents, coding tools, vertical copilots, and enterprise search where a small team can reach revenue inside a batch.

thesis.heading: Developer tooling as a repeat pattern
thesis.body: Speech, evaluation, memory and fine-tuning infrastructure recur batch after batch — Deepgram, AssemblyAI, Vellum, OpenPipe and Mem0 all sell picks and shovels to other AI builders, a category YC has funded for a decade.

thesis.heading: Standard terms as the real product
thesis.body: The uniform deal and Demo Day remove price negotiation from the earliest stage. For founders the value is access to 1,000+ investors on a fixed date; for YC it is the ability to originate at scale without competing on valuation.

portfolioGroups.heading: AI portfolio
portfolioGroups.blurb: A selection of YC-backed AI companies, from autonomy and data labelling to the voice, memory and evaluation tooling layers.

companies.name: Scale AI
companies.note: Data labelling and evaluation infrastructure for frontier labs and defence programmes; YC S16.

companies.name: Cruise
companies.note: Self-driving vehicle developer acquired by General Motors; the batch's earliest large autonomy outcome. YC W14.

companies.name: Deepgram
companies.note: Speech-to-text and voice agent APIs sold to contact centres and voice product teams. YC W16.

companies.name: AssemblyAI
companies.note: Speech recognition and audio intelligence models delivered as a developer API. YC S17.

companies.name: Ironclad
companies.note: Contract lifecycle platform that added model-driven review and redlining to legal workflows. YC W15.

companies.name: Speak
companies.note: AI language tutor using speech models for open-ended conversation practice. YC S16.

companies.name: Vapi
companies.note: Developer platform for building and deploying real-time voice agents.

companies.name: Retell AI
companies.note: Voice agent infrastructure for inbound and outbound phone operations.

companies.name: Vellum
companies.note: Prompt management, evaluation and deployment tooling for LLM applications.

companies.name: OpenPipe
companies.note: Fine-tuning and distillation platform that converts prompt traffic into cheaper task-specific models.

companies.name: Mem0
companies.note: Open-source memory layer giving agents persistent, retrievable user context.

companies.name: Onyx
companies.note: Open-source enterprise search and chat over internal company knowledge; formerly Danswer.
